question: In all of the following enzyme deficiencies, hyperammonemia is a common feature, EXCEPT:
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency" -> "impaired conversion of citrulline and aspartate to argininosuccinate" -> "increased ammonia levels" -> "hyperammonemia" -> 95%
CHAIN: "Carbamoyl Phosphate synthetase (CPS-I) deficiency" -> "reduced urea cycle function" -> "accumulation of ammonia" -> "hyperammonemia" -> 90%
CHAIN: "Ornithine transcarbamoylase (OTC) deficiency" -> "disruption of the urea cycle" -> "increased ammonia production" -> "hyperammonemia" -> 90%
CHAIN: "Ornithine amino transferase deficiency" -> "possible alternative metabolic pathway" -> "less direct impact on ammonia levels" -> "unclear effect on hyperammonemia" -> 70%
analysis: In evaluating the enzyme deficiencies listed, we can analyze their relationship with hyperammonemia. Argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency leads to an accumulation of ammonia due to impaired conversion of citrulline and aspartate to argininosuccinate, resulting in hyperammonemia. Carbamoyl Phosphate synthetase (CPS-I) deficiency also results in hyperammonemia due to reduced urea cycle function, leading to ammonia accumulation. Ornithine transcarbamoylase (OTC) deficiency disrupts the urea cycle, causing increased ammonia levels and hyperammonemia. However, ornithine amino transferase deficiency (also known as ornithine transaminase deficiency) is less directly associated with hyperammonemia. While it can lead to some metabolic disturbances, it does not typically cause significant hyperammonemia compared to the other three deficiencies. Therefore, the correct answer is that ornithine amino transferase deficiency is the exception among the listed options regarding hyperammonemia.
